name: Pediatric safe corridors for distal-femur spanning external fixation
aliases: pediatric femur tibia pin safe zones
corridor: Anterolateral or direct-lateral femoral and anteromedial tibial percutaneous pin corridors

positioning.text: Position supine with the full limb accessible and imageable from femur through tibia.

setup.text: Map both physes, soft-tissue injury, neurovascular anatomy, and future fixation paths before placing any pin.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark femoral shaft, distal-femoral physis, vastus lateralis, iliotibial band, fibular head, tibial crest, and planned definitive incisions.

incision.text: Use adequate small incisions and blunt dissection to bone to prevent skin and muscle tethering.

superficial_interval.text: Approach femur between rectus and vastus lateralis or directly lateral while avoiding iliotibial tract; approach tibia about 1 cm medial to the crest.

deep_interval.text: Use sleeves to bone, obtain controlled bicortical purchase without medial femoral plunge, and angle tibial pins approximately 20 degrees from sagittal away from posterolateral structures.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, anterior-lateral thigh muscle to femur; skin and subcutaneous tissue directly to anteromedial tibia.

structures_encountered.text: Rectus-vastus interval, vastus lateralis, femoral periosteum, tibial crest, and anteromedial tibial cortex are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Distal-femoral physis, medial femoral vessels, sciatic nerve, common and deep peroneal nerves, anterior tibial vessels, saphenous nerve, and definitive operative planes are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep distal femoral pins at least 2 cm proximal to the physis; avoid medial overpenetration, fibular-head pinning, and posterolateral tibial trajectories.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid iliotibial-band tethering, thermal necrosis, drill plunge, and tight skin around pins.

exposure.text: Provides pediatric-safe skeletal purchase for temporary stabilization while preserving growth plates and definitive fixation corridors.

limitations.text: Published safe zones remain guides; patient size, fracture displacement, soft-tissue injury, and physeal location require individual imaging.

extensions.text: Add or relocate pins only after remapping physes and neurovascular and definitive-treatment corridors.

indications.text: Use for staged damage-control stabilization of unstable pediatric distal-femur injuries when definitive treatment must be delayed.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid injured or infected skin and any corridor where the physis or neurovascular anatomy cannot be reliably localized.

implant_implications.text: Keep pins outside the future nail, plate, and incision paths and preserve sufficient distance from fracture and physis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal clearance, bicortical purchase without overpenetration, joint clearance, and frame alignment on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Release tethered skin, dress pin sites, and document distal perfusion and nerve function after frame construction.

complications.text: Complications include physeal injury, neurovascular injury, pin-track infection, thermal injury, fracture propagation, stiffness, and contamination of definitive corridors.

bailouts.text: If physis or safe trajectory is uncertain, stop and relocate under imaging or direct exposure rather than accepting a hazardous pin.

procedure_applications.condition: Temporary knee-spanning stabilization is required with protection of physes, neurovascular structures, and definitive surgical corridors

Why avoid the iliotibial tract?
questions.answer: To reduce loosening and pin-track infection from tethered motion.
